#1
L: Mind attached to me, O son of Pṛthā, practicing yoga, having me as refuge — without doubt, completely, how you shall know me, that hear.
I: With your mind fixed on me, Pārtha, practicing yoga and relying on me, hear now how you shall know me completely, beyond all doubt.
N: This opens Kṛṣṇa's discourse proper, continuing without interruption from the end of chapter 6, and addressed throughout this chapter to Arjuna as Pārtha, 'son of Pṛthā' (i.e. Kuntī). Sandhi: मय्यासक्तमनाः is mayi + āsakta-manāḥ (i + ā → yā); तच्छृणु is tat + śṛṇu (-t + ś- → -c ch-). Mad-āśrayaḥ, 'having me as refuge', anticipates the theme of surrender to Kṛṣṇa alone that runs through the whole chapter (cf. verse 14's māṃ eva ye prapadyante).
#2
L: Knowledge, together with discernment, to you I shall speak, this, completely; having known which, nothing further, other, here remains to be known.
I: I will teach you this knowledge in full, together with its realization, leaving nothing out; once you have known it, nothing further remains to be known here.
N: Jñāna and vijñāna, 'knowledge' and 'discernment' (its personally realized counterpart, per Śaṅkara — cf. 6.8's jñāna-vijñāna-tṛpta-ātmā), give this chapter its title, Jñāna-vijñāna-yoga; the promise that nothing further remains to be known once this teaching is grasped is fulfilled by the chapter's own subject, Kṛṣṇa's full nature. Sandhi: तेऽहं is te + aham; सविज्ञानमिदं is sa-vijñānam + idam (no fusion — final -m stays before a vowel); वक्ष्याम्यशेषतः is vakṣyāmi + aśeṣataḥ; यज्ज्ञात्वा is yat + jñātvā; नेह is na + iha; भूयोऽन्यज्ज्ञातव्यमवशिष्यते packs bhūyaḥ + anyat + jñātavyam + avaśiṣyate.
#3
L: Among thousands of men, someone strives for perfection; even among those striving [and] perfected, someone knows me in truth.
I: Among thousands of men, scarcely one strives for perfection; and even among those who strive and succeed, scarcely one knows me in truth.
N: Kaścit ... kaścit, 'someone ... someone', doubled, understates the rarity rather than saying 'few' outright — tradition reads it as 'hardly anyone at all'. Sandhi: कश्चिद्यतति is kaścit + yatati (-t + y- → -d y-); कश्चिन्मां is kaścit + mām (-t + m- → -n m-).
#4
L: Earth, water, fire, air, ether, mind, and understanding too, and egoism — thus this, my nature, divided, eightfold.
I: Earth, water, fire, air, ether, mind, understanding, and egoism — this is my nature, divided eight ways.
N: The first formal statement of prakṛti as eightfold: five gross elements (bhūmi, ap, anala, vāyu, kha), then manas, buddhi, and ahaṃkāra, 'ego, the sense of I' — together Kṛṣṇa's 'lower' nature, set against the 'higher' nature named in the next verse. Note that ahaṃkāra is here classed as a product of nature, not as the self. Sandhi across the list: bhūmiḥ+āpaḥ→bhūmir āpaḥ; āpaḥ+analaḥ→āpo'nalaḥ; manaḥ+buddhiḥ→mano buddhiḥ; buddhiḥ+eva→buddhir eva; iti+iyam→itīyam; prakṛtiḥ+aṣṭadhā→prakṛtir aṣṭadhā.
#5
L: This is the lower; but know as another, different [from] this, my higher nature — become the individual soul, O mighty-armed one, by which this world is sustained.
I: This is my lower nature; but know that I have another, higher nature besides it — the very principle of life, mighty-armed Arjuna, by which this universe is sustained.
N: Parā prakṛti, the 'higher nature', is defined as jīva-bhūtā, 'become the individual soul' — Śaṅkara identifies it with the kṣetrajña, the knower of the field, taken up at length in chapter 13 — and is set against the aparā, 'lower', eightfold material nature of verse 4. Sandhi: अपरेयमितस्त्वन्यां packs aparā + iyam (ā+i→e), + itaḥ, itaḥ+tu→itastu, tu+anyām→tvanyām (yaṇ sandhi, u→v); ययेदं is yayā + idam (ā+i→e).
#6
L: Having this as their source, all beings — thus understand; I of the whole world [am] the origin, and likewise the dissolution.
I: Understand that all beings have their source in this twofold nature of mine; I am the origin of the whole world, and its dissolution as well.
N: Etad-yonīni, 'having this as their source', sums up verses 4-5: everything that exists arises from Kṛṣṇa's own nature in both its aspects, lower and higher. Sandhi: एतद्योनीनि is etat + yoni (-t + y- → -d y-); सर्वाणीत्युपधारय packs sarvāṇi + iti + upadhāraya (i+i→ī; i+u→y u-); प्रलयस्तथा is pralayaḥ + tathā.
#7
L: Than me higher nothing else whatsoever exists, Winner-of-wealth; in me all this is strung, as clusters of jewels on a thread.
I: There is nothing whatsoever higher than me, Dhanaṃjaya; on me all this is strung, like clusters of jewels on a thread.
N: Dhanaṃjaya, 'winner of wealth', an epithet of Arjuna won for plundering wealth from defeated kings, first occurs in this chapter here. The image of jewels strung on a thread (sūtre maṇi-gaṇāḥ iva) pictures the whole cosmos as held together by, and wholly dependent on, Kṛṣṇa as its one underlying support — concrete confirmation of verse 6's claim to be the origin and dissolution of everything. Sandhi: नान्यत्किंचिदस्ति packs na + anyat + kiṃcit + asti (a+a→ā; -t+a→-d a-).
#8
L: Sap I am in the waters, O son of Kuntī; light I am of moon and sun; the syllable Om in all the Vedas, sound in ether, manliness in men.
I: I am the taste in water, Kaunteya; I am the radiance of the moon and the sun; I am the syllable Om in all the Vedas, the sound in space, the manly vigor in men.
N: A catalogue of self-manifestations opens here and runs through verse 11, each an instance of 'I am' (made explicit only once, in prabhāsmi). Praṇava, 'Om', is the syllable that opens Vedic recitation; śabda, 'sound', is traditionally the defining quality of ether (ākāśa) among the five elements. Sandhi: रसोऽहमप्सु is rasaḥ + aham + apsu; प्रभास्मि is prabhā + asmi.
#9
L: Pure fragrance in the earth, and radiance I am in fire; life in all beings, and austerity I am in ascetics.
I: I am the pure fragrance in the earth and the brilliance in fire; I am the life in all beings and the austerity in ascetics.
N: Continues verse 8's catalogue with four more instances. Vibhāvasu, literally 'possessing splendor', is a standing epithet used as a name for Agni, fire. Sandhi: तेजश्चास्मि and तपश्चास्मि both pack X + ca + asmi (-aḥ+c-→-aś c-; ca+asmi→cāsmi).
#10
L: The seed of all beings, know me, O son of Pṛthā, [as] eternal; the intellect of the intelligent I am, the brilliance of the brilliant [am] I.
I: Know me, Pārtha, to be the eternal seed of all beings; I am the intellect of the intelligent, and the brilliance of the brilliant.
N: Bīja, 'seed', is the causal image of Kṛṣṇa as the eternal seed from which all beings grow, resumed at 9.18 and 14.4. Sandhi: बुद्धिर्बुद्धिमतामस्मि is buddhiḥ + buddhimatām + asmi (-iḥ+b-→-ir b-); तेजस्तेजस्विनामहम् is tejaḥ + tejasvinām + aham (-aḥ+t-→-as t-), aham here carrying the sense of the asmi already used in the first half.
#11
L: The strength of the strong, and I [am, that strength] free from desire and attachment; not opposed to dharma among beings, desire I am, O bull among the Bharatas.
I: And I am the strength of the strong, free from desire and passion; and in all beings I am the desire that is not opposed to dharma, bull among the Bharatas.
N: Bharatarṣabha, 'bull among the descendants of Bharata', an epithet of Arjuna, first occurs in this chapter here (sandhi bharata+ṛṣabha→bharatarṣabha, a+ṛ-→ar-). The verse distinguishes ordinary desire (kāma) — condemned elsewhere as the enemy, 3.37, 2.62-63 — from kāma dharma-aviruddhaḥ, 'desire not opposed to dharma', legitimate desire pursued within the bounds of right order, which Kṛṣṇa here claims as his own. Sandhi: चाहं is ca+aham; धर्माविरुद्धो is dharma+aviruddhaḥ; कामोऽस्मि is kāmaḥ+asmi.
#12
L: Which indeed are states of sattva, and of rajas and of tamas — know them as from me alone; but I [am] not in them, they [are] in me.
I: Whatever states of being there are — of sattva, of rajas, or of tamas — know that all of them come from me alone; but I am not in them; they are in me.
N: Sāttvika, rājasa, tāmasa, formed from the three guṇas, are the poem's first mention of all three together by name, ahead of their systematic treatment from chapter 14 on; guṇa and its derivatives stay untranslated per convention. The paradox mattaḥ eva ... na tv ahaṃ teṣu, 'from me alone ... yet I am not in them', is developed in the next verse and echoes the fuller formula at 9.4-5. Sandhi: चैव is ca+eva; राजसास्तामसाश्च is rājasāḥ+tāmasāḥ+ca; मत्त एवेति is mattaḥ+eva+iti (visarga silently dropped before the vowel of eva); त्वहं is tu+aham (yaṇ sandhi, u→v).
#13
L: By these three states made of the guṇas, all this world, deluded, does not recognize me, beyond these, the supreme, the imperishable.
I: Deluded by these three states made of the guṇas, this whole world fails to recognize me, who am beyond them, supreme and imperishable.
N: Guṇa-mayaiḥ bhāvaiḥ, 'states made of the guṇas', names the sāttvika, rājasa and tāmasa states of verse 12; guṇa stays untranslated while the suffix '-maya' ('made of, consisting of') is translated. The verse states the paradox of verse 12 from the world's side: deceived by what the guṇas produce, it fails to recognize Kṛṣṇa as param avyayam, 'beyond these, imperishable' — the veiling power named directly as māyā in the next verse. Sandhi: त्रिभिर्गुणमयैर्भावैरेभिः packs tribhiḥ+guṇamayaiḥ+bhāvaiḥ+ebhiḥ; नाभिजानाति is na+abhijānāti.
#14
L: Divine indeed [is] this, made of the guṇas, my illusion, hard to cross over; me alone who resort to, this illusion they cross over, they.
I: This divine illusion of mine, made of the guṇas, is hard to overcome; but those who take refuge in me alone cross over this illusion.
N: Māyā, rendered 'illusion' per Monier-Williams, is deliberately translated here — unlike guṇa, dharma, yoga, brahman and sāṃkhya, which stay untranslated: daivī ... guṇamayī māyā, 'this divine illusion of mine, made of the guṇas', names the veiling power that verse 13 described impersonally, now claimed as Kṛṣṇa's own (mama) and called durat-yayā, 'hard to cross over'. The one way past it is stated directly, māṃ eva ye prapadyante, 'those who take refuge in me alone', anticipating the fourfold classification of devotees beginning at verse 16. Sandhi: ह्येषा is hi+eṣā (i+e→ye, yaṇ sandhi).
#15
L: Not me evil-doers, deluded, lowest of men, resort to — by illusion robbed of knowledge, having resorted to a demonic nature.
I: Evil-doers do not resort to me — deluded men, the lowest of mankind, their knowledge robbed by illusion, given over to a demonic nature.
N: This gives the negative counterpart to verse 14's promise: duṣkṛtinaḥ, 'evil-doers', are māyayā apahṛta-jñānāḥ, 'whose knowledge illusion has carried off' — the same illusion of verse 14, here at its most destructive — because they have instead āsuraṃ bhāvam āśritāḥ, 'taken refuge in a demonic nature', foreshadowing the fuller contrast of divine and demonic natures in chapter 16. Sandhi: दुष्कृतिनो is duṣkṛtinaḥ (-aḥ before m-→-o); नराधमाः is nara+adhamāḥ (a+a→ā); माययापहृतज्ञाना is māyayā+apahṛta-jñānāḥ.
#16
L: Fourfold worship me, people meritorious, O Arjuna: the distressed, the desirous-of-knowledge, the seeker-of-gain, and the man of knowledge, O bull among the Bharatas.
I: Four kinds of virtuous people worship me, Arjuna: the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the man of wisdom, bull among the Bharatas.
N: This opens the classic fourfold classification of devotees, developed through verse 19: ārta, 'the distressed'; jijñāsu, 'one desiring to know'; artha-arthī, 'one seeking [worldly] gain'; and jñānī, 'the man of knowledge' — all called sukṛtinaḥ, 'of good deeds', since even self-interested worship of Kṛṣṇa presupposes merit. Sandhi: सुकृतिनोऽर्जुन is sukṛtinaḥ+arjuna; जिज्ञासुरर्थार्थी packs jijñāsuḥ+artha+arthī.
#17
L: Of these, the man of knowledge, ever disciplined, of single devotion, excels; dear indeed to the man of knowledge exceedingly [am] I, and he [is] dear to me.
I: Of these, the man of knowledge, ever disciplined and singly devoted, is supreme; for I am exceedingly dear to the man of knowledge, and he is dear to me.
N: This ranks the jñānī highest of the four types named in verse 16, describing him as nitya-yuktaḥ eka-bhaktiḥ, 'constantly disciplined, of single-minded devotion'; the mutual bond of dearness (priyaḥ ... priyaḥ) between Kṛṣṇa and the wise devotee is pressed further in verse 18 and echoes the later catalogue of 12.14-20. Sandhi: एकभक्तिर्विशिष्यते is eka-bhaktiḥ+viśiṣyate; ज्ञानिनोऽत्यर्थमहं is jñāninaḥ+atyartham+aham.
#18
L: Noble indeed [are] all these; but the man of knowledge — [he is] my very self, [that is] my view; he, for, of disciplined self, is grounded in me alone [as] the highest goal.
I: All of these are noble, but the man of knowledge I hold to be my very self; for he, his self disciplined, is grounded in me alone as the highest goal.
N: This ranks the jñānī above the other three types of verse 16 in the strongest terms yet: ātmā eva me matam, 'he is, in my view, my very self' — identity language beyond even verse 17's mutual dearness. A textual note: the expected pronominal plural sarve, agreeing with ete, 'these', here appears in the manuscript tradition as bare sarva; the sense, 'all of these', is unaffected. Sandhi: एवैते is eva+ete (a+e→ai); त्वात्मैव is tu+ātmā+eva (yaṇ sandhi u→v; ā+e→ai); मामेवानुत्तमां is mām+eva+anuttamām (a+a→ā).
#19
L: At the end of many births, the man of knowledge resorts to me, [thinking] 'the son of Vasudeva is everything' — thus; he, the great-souled one, is very hard to find.
I: After many births, the wise man takes refuge in me, realizing that Vāsudeva is everything; such a great soul is very rare.
N: Vāsudevaḥ sarvam iti, 'the son of Vasudeva is everything' (or 'all this is Vāsudeva'), is the chapter's most quoted line: Kṛṣṇa's own patronymic, Vāsudeva, is here identified with the totality of existence — the culminating realization of the jñānī praised in verses 17-18. Sandhi: सर्वमिति is sarvam+iti; स is saḥ before m- (visarga dropped).
#20
L: By these and those desires robbed of knowledge, they resort to other deities, having adopted this or that observance, constrained by their own nature.
I: Those whose understanding is carried off by one desire or another resort to other deities, adopting this or that observance, driven by their own nature.
N: This turns to worship of 'other deities' as the counterpart to the jñānī's realization in verse 19: kāmaiḥ taiḥ taiḥ hṛta-jñānāḥ, 'whose knowledge is carried off by these various desires', echoes verse 15's māyayā apahṛta-jñānāḥ, but here the cause is named as desire rather than illusion outright, and the outcome is not irreligion but its diversion toward lesser objects — still ultimately Kṛṣṇa's own doing, as the next verse explains. Sandhi: कामैस्तैस्तैर्हृतज्ञानाः packs kāmaiḥ+taiḥ+taiḥ+hṛta-jñānāḥ; प्रपद्यन्तेऽन्यदेवताः is prapadyante+anya-devatāḥ.
#21
L: Whatever devotee whatever form with faith wishes to worship, of that one that unwavering faith, that very [faith] I make firm, I.
I: Whatever form any devotee wishes to worship with faith, that very faith of his I make firm and unwavering.
N: Yo yo ... yāṃ yāṃ ... tasya tasya, doubled relatives across both lines, are the standard Sanskrit distributive construction, 'whoever ... whatever ... of each such person': whatever deity's form a devotee approaches with faith, Kṛṣṇa himself is the one who grants and steadies that faith — the doctrine behind verse 20's worship of other deities. Sandhi: श्रद्धयार्चितुमिच्छति packs śraddhayā+arcitum+icchati; तस्याचलां is tasya+acalām (a+a→ā); विदधाम्यहम् is vidadhāmi+aham (-i+a→-y a-).
#22
L: He, endowed with that faith, seeks the worship of that [deity], and obtains thereby [his] desires, granted by me alone indeed, those.
I: Endowed with that faith, he seeks to worship that deity, and thereby obtains what he desires — desires granted, in truth, by me alone.
N: This continues verse 21: the devotee, steadied in faith, does obtain what he seeks from the lesser deity, but the verse insists mayaiva vihitān, 'granted by me alone' — that the fruit of any such worship still ultimately comes from Kṛṣṇa, the hidden source behind every deity, a claim made explicit in the next verse. Sandhi: युक्तस्तस्याराधनमीहते packs yuktaḥ+tasya+ārādhanam+īhate; कामान्मयैव is kāmān+mayā+eva (ā+e→ai).
#23
L: Finite, however, [is] the fruit of them; that comes to be for those of little intelligence; the worshippers of the gods go to the gods, my devotees go to me also.
I: But the fruit for such people is finite; it belongs to those of little intelligence: worshippers of the gods go to the gods, but my devotees come to me.
N: This states plainly what verses 20-22 implied: worship of 'other deities', though ultimately granted through Kṛṣṇa, yields only antavat phalam, 'a finite result', fit for alpa-medhasām, 'those of little understanding' — contrasted with mad-bhaktāḥ, 'my devotees', who reach Kṛṣṇa himself rather than a lesser heaven. Sandhi: अन्तवत्तु is antavat+tu; तद्भवत्यल्पमेधसाम् packs tat+bhavati+alpa-medhasām; देवान्देवयजो is devān+deva-yajaḥ; मद्भक्ता is mat+bhaktāḥ.
#24
L: The unmanifest, having attained manifestation, unwise men think of me — not knowing my higher state, imperishable, unsurpassed.
I: Unwise men think of me, the unmanifest, as having come into manifest existence — not knowing my higher nature, imperishable and unsurpassed.
N: This criticizes those who take Kṛṣṇa's avatāra-appearance (cf. 4.6's ātma-māyā) for an ordinary change from unmanifest to manifest, missing his param bhāvam, 'higher nature' — avyayam anuttamam, 'imperishable, unsurpassed' — which no apparent birth touches, a point sharpened in verse 25's nāhaṃ prakāśaḥ sarvasya. Sandhi: ममाव्ययमनुत्तमम् packs mama+avyayam+anuttamam (a+a→ā).
#25
L: Not I [am] manifest to all, veiled by [my] power of illusion exercised through yoga; this deluded world does not recognize me, unborn, imperishable.
I: I am not manifest to all, veiled as I am by my power of illusion exercised through yoga; this deluded world does not recognize me, the unborn, the imperishable.
N: Yoga-māyā, 'the power of illusion exercised through yoga', names the mechanism behind verse 24's error: Kṛṣṇa is hidden from ordinary sight not by any real birth or change but by his own concealing power, called māyā at verse 14 and here specified as wielded through yoga. Ajam avyayam, 'unborn, imperishable', restates verse 24's avyayam anuttamam in the poem's standard terms for what undergoes no birth or change, echoing 4.6's ajaḥ api san. Sandhi: नाहं is na+aham; मूढोऽयं is mūḍhaḥ+ayam; नाभिजानाति is na+abhijānāti.
#26
L: I know past, present, and future beings, Arjuna; but me no one at all knows.
I: I know all beings, Arjuna — past, present and to come; but no one knows me.
N: Vedāham ... na tu veda kaścana plays on two senses of vid, 'to know': Kṛṣṇa's own knowledge spans all three times, yet he himself remains unknown to anyone — the same hiddenness as verses 24-25, now stated as a general asymmetry rather than a matter of illusion specifically, and the premise for verses 27-30 on how ignorance of him arises and is overcome. Sandhi: वेदाहं is veda+aham (a+a→ā); चार्जुन is ca+arjuna (a+a→ā).
#27
L: By the delusion of the pairs of opposites, arising from desire and aversion, O descendant of Bharata, all beings fall into delusion at [their] birth, O scorcher of the foe.
I: All beings fall into delusion at birth, Bhārata, through the delusion of opposites that arises from desire and aversion, scorcher of the foe.
N: Bhārata and Parantapa, both epithets of Arjuna, first occur in this chapter here. Dvandva, 'the pair, duality' — the opposites like pleasure and pain, heat and cold, cf. 2.14's śītoṣṇa-sukha-duḥkha — arises from icchā-dveṣa, 'desire and aversion', and this dvandva-moha, 'delusion of opposites', is named as the root cause of every being's bewilderment sarge, 'at birth, at [each] creation' — the ordinary condition from which the devotees of verse 28 are freed.
#28
L: But of whom the sin has come to an end, of people of meritorious deeds — they, freed from the delusion of the pairs of opposites, worship me, of firm vow.
I: But those people of meritorious deeds whose sin has come to an end, freed from the delusion of opposites, worship me with firm resolve.
N: This gives the positive counterpart to verse 27: janānām puṇya-karmaṇām, 'people of meritorious deeds', whose pāpam antagatam, 'sin has run its course', become dvandva-moha-nirmuktāḥ, 'freed from the delusion of opposites' just described, and so can worship Kṛṣṇa dṛḍha-vratāḥ, 'with firm vows'. Sandhi: त्वन्तगतं is tu+anta-gatam (yaṇ sandhi, u→v).
#29
L: For release from old age and death, having taken refuge in me, those who strive — they know that brahman entire, the whole [truth of] the individual self, and action entirely.
I: Those who strive for release from old age and death, taking refuge in me, come to know brahman completely, the whole truth of the individual self, and action in its entirety.
N: Adhyātma, 'pertaining to the self, the individual self', is a technical term defined explicitly at the opening of the next chapter (8.3); here, alongside brahman (kept untranslated) and karman, 'action', it names one of the domains of complete knowledge reached by those who take refuge in Kṛṣṇa for jarā-maraṇa-mokṣa, 'release from old age and death'. This verse and the next set up, ahead of their full definition, the further terms adhibhūta and adhidaiva that open chapter 8. Sandhi: मामाश्रित्य is mām+āśritya; तद्विदुः is tat+viduḥ (-t+v-→-d v-); चाखिलम् is ca+akhilam (a+a→ā).
#30
L: Together with the elements and the divine order, me, together with sacrifice too, who know — even at the time of departure, me they know, of disciplined mind.
I: Those who know me together with the elements, the divine order, and sacrifice — being of disciplined mind, they know me even at the time of death.
N: This closes the chapter with the third technical term, adhiyajña, 'pertaining to sacrifice' (with adhibhūta and adhidaiva from verse 29); all three are given their full definitions only at the start of chapter 8, whose opening question from Arjuna repeats these very words. Prayāṇa-kāle, 'at the time of departure [from the body]', i.e. at death, names the ultimate test of this knowledge, developed at length in chapter 8's teaching on what is remembered at the moment of death. Sandhi: साधिभूताधिदैवं packs sa+adhibhūta+adhidaivam (a+a→ā twice); साधियज्ञं is sa+adhiyajñam (a+a→ā); प्रयाणकालेऽपि is kāle+api; विदुर्युक्तचेतसः is viduḥ+yukta-cetasaḥ (-uḥ+y-→-ur y-).
